facts.text: The Madrid metro is extensive and cheap, arguably the easiest way to move around given the major sights are more spread out than in more compact cities like Florence.

The Spanish dining schedule runs late - lunch is often 2-4pm and dinner rarely starts before 9pm; restaurants that look "closed" mid-afternoon are frequently just on their siesta break, not shut for the day.
Restaurants directly on Plaza Mayor are a well-known overpriced tourist zone; La Latina and Malasaña a short walk away offer both better tapas and better prices.
The Prado, Reina Sofía, and Thyssen-Bornemisza museums each have specific free-entry windows (typically a few hours in the evening) - worth checking current hours if budget-conscious.
Many smaller Madrid bars and tapas spots are cash-preferred, especially for small tabs.

Traditional Madrid cuisine is meat-and-seafood heavy (jamón, cocido madrileño, callos); vegetarian tapas are common as a category (patatas bravas, pimientos, tortilla) even at traditional bars, more so than in some other Spanish cities.
